newsitem.title: HONG KONG: PRESS DIGEST-Hong Kong newspaper headlines-May 6.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST-Hong Kong newspaper headlines-May 6.

text.p: These are some of the leading stories in the Hong Kong press on Tuesday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
-- MING PAO -- Britain's new Labour government stressed that a successful handover of Hong Kong to China on July 1 was one of its priorities.
-- Chinese vice-premier Qian Qichen invited post-handover leader Tung Chee-hwa to visit Beijing on Wednesday to discuss handover issues.
-- SING TAO -- In 20 years, Hong Kong's population will have increased by 1.8 million to 8.21 million people, with more than half of them mainland Chinese immigrants.

-- APPLE DAILY -- Some members of the post-handover Executive Council, or inner cabinet, were actively promoting a ministerial system. They had suggested offering compensation to persuade senior government officials to retire, making it easier for Tung to restructure his team to exclude those with different opinions.

-- TIN TIN DAILY -- China is concerned about the worsening crime situation in Macau and had sent more than 20 senior officials to the Portugese-run enclave to resolve conflicts between rival organised criminal gangs.
-- ECONOMIC TIMES -- The chairman of China's securities and futures commission said Hong Kong would become a gathering centre for Chinese enterprises seeking listings overseas.
-- SOUTH CHINA MORNING POST -- The ceremony marking Hong Kong's return to China will begin half an hour before midnight on June 30 and last up to 45 minutes.

-- Investors pumped more than 30 billion yuan into the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock markets on Monday, lifting share prices to their highest levels since "China fever" gripped international and local investors in late 1993 and early 1994.

-- HONGKONG STANDARD -- Members of the post-handover Executive Council were scheduled to debate the definition of a "political organisation" before they decided on concessions they could make on proposed changes to Hong Kong's civil liberties laws.
